That arrangement can work well while you're using the service.
Then the show ends, the project finishes, or your needs change.
The renewal keeps doing exactly what it was designed to do.
Now you have to notice the charge, find the cancellation process and finish it before another payment.
Otherwise, the subscription can continue even though the reason you joined has disappeared.
This is the power of a default.
What happens when you don't make another choice?
For a one -time rental, the default is that the transaction ends.
For an automatically renewing subscription, the default is that it continues.
The effort falls in a different place.
Researchers found a useful way to examine that difference.
They studied payment card data for 10 subscription services, looking at what happened when customers' cards were replaced.
Replacements could interrupt the usual payment and require customers to take an active step to continue.
Cancellation rates rose around those replacement months.
The data doesn't reveal every customer's reasons.
Some may have forgotten a service.
Others may have reconsidered its value.
The researchers modeled inattention and cancellation costs, and their estimates depend on the services and assumptions they studied.
But the finding shows why an automatic payment matters.
Interrupt the payment, and some customers make a different choice.
Of course, remembering the subscription is only the first step.
You still have to leave.
Imagine a large button labeled Keep Membership with a smaller link underneath to continue cancelling.
You decline a discount, pass a reminder of the features you'll lose and reach an offer to pause instead.

Each screen creates another moment where the process can stop, a meeting starts, you close the page, or you think the last button completed the cancellation when there's another confirmation below it.
If you haven't finished, the default may carry on.
Researchers examining news subscriptions across several countries documented barriers including requirements to call a representative or type of phrase.
Those examples don't describe every service.
They show how a choice can be available while still taking effort to carry out.
That effort isn't equally easy for everyone.
A phone call during office hours can be difficult for someone working shifts or caring for family.

Just cancel it assumes that deciding to leave and successfully leaving are practically the same task for the company The two tasks can have very different outcomes a completed cancellation ends future subscription payments a postponed Cancellation can leave the next charge in place that gives a business a reason to pay attention to every step between the customer's decision And the final confirmation, but a discount might actually help the customer
Why shouldn't a company offer one?
It can.
A lower price may make a service worthwhile, and a pause may suit someone who plans to return.
The issue is whether declining those offers and finishing the cancellation remains clear and straightforward.
Regulators and researchers use the term dark pattern for certain designs that mislead people or steer their choices.
Obscuring a cancellation option can be one example.
A useful confirmation screen by itself isn't evidence of deception.
The distinction is what the design helps the customer do.
In 2023, the United States Federal Trade Commission sued Amazon over prime enrollment and cancellation practices.
The FTC alleged that Amazon enrolled millions of consumers without informed consent and made cancellation difficult.
Amazon contested the allegations and the case was later settled.
An older cancellation process described in the case allegedly required four screens and six clicks, with reminders and a pause option along the way.
In 2025, Amazon agreed to a settlement including a $1 billion civil penalty and $1 .5 billion for consumer redress alongside changes to its enrollment and cancellation practices.
